name: Ursa Minor
introduction: is the Little Bear, also known as the Little Dipper: a small and mostly faint constellation with an outsized role. The end of its handle is Polaris, the North Star. For observers in the Northern Hemisphere, the whole sky appears to turn around this point, and from mid-northern latitudes the Little Dipper never sets.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: [Polaris](hip:11767) lies less than a degree from the north celestial pole, the point in the sky directly above Earth’s North Pole. As other stars rise and set, it stays almost still, and its height above the horizon roughly equals your latitude. For centuries, sailors used this to find their way north and estimate how far north they were.

Polaris has not always been the pole star, and it will not remain so. Earth’s axis slowly wobbles like a spinning top, tracing a circle in the sky about every 26,000 years. When the pyramids of Egypt were built, the pole lay near Thuban in Draco; in about 12,000 years it will be near brilliant Vega in Lyra.

image.caption: Star View schematic · catalogue positions, approximate pole-star epochs
image.alt: The north celestial pole traces a circle around the ecliptic pole over about 26,000 years, passing Thuban, Polaris, Errai, Deneb and Vega.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Polaris](hip:11767) is not the brightest star in the sky, but it is a remarkable one: a yellow supergiant about 430 light-years away, with two smaller companions. It is also the nearest Cepheid variable, gently pulsing in brightness every four days.

[Kochab](hip:72607) and [Pherkad](hip:75097), at the end of the bowl, are known as the Guardians of the Pole because they circle Polaris like sentries. Kochab, an orange giant about 130 light-years away, has a planet several times Jupiter’s mass. Around 1000 BC, before Polaris had drifted close to the pole, Kochab was the brighter guide to north. The other stars of the Little Dipper, such as [Yildun](hip:85822), are faint enough that light pollution often hides them.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: Around December 22, the Ursid meteor shower, produced by debris from Comet 8P/Tuttle, radiates from near Kochab. Much farther away lies the Ursa Minor Dwarf, a faint satellite galaxy of the Milky Way about 250,000 light-years away, made almost entirely of very old stars.
